newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS- Russia-Belarus monetary union still far away.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS- Russia-Belarus monetary union still far away.

text.p: Russia and Belarus promised to make their two economies the focus of a Union Treaty signed on Wednesday, but admitted that merging two systems and creating a single currency were still far away.

"The kernel of the Union is economy. We have to do everything to rebuild economic links between the two countries," Russian President Boris Yeltsin said before he signed the document with Belarussian leader Alexander Lukashenko.

But Yeltsin said much work was needed before the two former Soviet republics could introduce a single currency and Russian Central Bank chief Sergei Dubinin said this would take years rather than months.

"The establishment of a union between the two states must be the initial stage of the creation of an integrated federal state which will also have common monetary and budgetary systems," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Dubinin as saying.
Monetary integration was "likely to take one or two years, not several months", he added.

Conservatives traumatised by the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union are keen on the union. But economists say the cost to Russia of merging with Belarus, which has made few reforms since the Soviet era, would be huge.

The treaty signed on Wednesday differs substantially from a draft prepared by Lukashenko and conservatives in the Russian administration. It calls vaguely for increased cooperation in many fields, including the economy.
Social-economic cooperation should use "market mechanisms", it says.

Russia and its western neighbour have followed very different economic paths since 1991. The market-oriented, newly-privatised Russian economy contrasts sharply with the tightly-controlled Belarussian one.
"Co-operation on a market basis between Russian and Belarus enterprises will start, and Russia and Belarus will speed up their drive out of the economic crisis," Yeltsin said.

Both the Russian and Belarussian economies were hit hard when the Soviet collapse disrupted trade ties and made it difficult for factories to get supplies and raw materials. But analysts have argued over the economic impact of union.

Conservatives say union will boost Russian customs revenues by closing a loophole under which goods from Ukraine and from central and western Europe enter Russia through its porous frontier to the west.

But liberals have warned that Russia could face a heavy bill if it allowed Belarussians to use the relatively stable Russian rouble instead of the almost worthless Belarussian currency, or if Russia had to subsidise Belarussian firms with budget funds.
Lukashenko said his country of 10 million would not be an expense for its bigger and more powerful neighbour.
Belarus had brought two billion roubles a year to the coffers of the former Soviet Union. "It will never be true that our small country will be a burden on Russia," he said.
Lukashenko said in an interview with Germany's ZDF television that the union with Russia met a global trend towards alliances of states with common economic and military aims.
"We want to be a unified customs and economic zone. In a few years we want to reach a level of integration comparable to that which exists in the European Union today," he said.

Yeltsin said the union would give an impulse to merging the monetary systems of the two countries, but he added: "We still have to do a lot to introduce a single currency... there is no room for illusion here."
Western economists say a monetary union could undermine the Russian rouble and re-ignite inflation.

"If monetary union happens it will have a one-off negative impact on the Russian economy, which is basically the last thing the Russian economy needs at the moment," said Roland Nash, chief economist at Renaissance Capital.
But he added: "There are enough people in the Russian government who understand the implications of economic union with Belarus to keep it off for the forseeable future."
